# Mutants that survive the test suite, and why each one is allowed to.
#
# `.github/workflows/mutants.yml` diffs this file against the survivors of a
# real campaign, in both directions. A survivor missing from here is a guard
# somebody lost. An entry here that no longer survives is a gap somebody closed
# while this file still claimed it was open. Both are red.
#
# FORMAT — one line per surviving mutation:
#
#     <count><TAB><path>: <the mutation cargo-mutants applied>
#
# The line and column are stripped on purpose and the count is what replaces
# them. `mutants.yml` explains that choice in full; the short version is that a
# key carrying a line number reds on a comment, and a gate that reds on a
# comment gets deleted.
#
# This file describes the RUST crate. The python hook pack has its own,
# unrelated mutation campaign in `hooks/tests/mutate.py`, and a count from that
# one says nothing about any line below.
#
# REGENERATE — dispatch the workflow. Do not hand-edit a line, re-derive it:
#
#     gh workflow run mutants.yml --ref <your-branch>
#     gh run watch "$(gh run list --workflow=mutants.yml --limit 1 \
#       --json databaseId --jq '.[0].databaseId')"
#
# With no `-f scope=…` the run uses the one scope this file describes. A run on
# any other scope is REPORTED and never diffed, so it cannot regenerate this.
#
# A run whose survivors differ from this file FAILS and uploads its evidence:
#
#     gh run download <run-id> -n mutants-run
#
# `mutants-run/mutants.out/missed.txt` is the raw list. Normalise it with the
# SAME three lines the workflow uses — the `NORMALISE` heredoc in
# `.github/workflows/mutants.yml` — and paste the result below, each line with
# its reason. A baseline produced by different code from the one that checks it
# is a baseline that reds on the day it lands. There is deliberately no artifact
# on a green run: a green run has nothing to regenerate from, because this file
# already matches.
#
# THIS COMMAND USED TO BE A LOCAL `cargo mutants` INVOCATION, and whoever read
# it ran one, which is the whole reason the line is now a dispatch. The campaign
# is about forty minutes of saturated CPU. On a workstation running many
# concurrent sessions behind one job queue it holds a slot for the whole of it
# while every other session's typecheck and test run waits behind it; measured,
# one local campaign held the queue eighty minutes with no output and another
# drove the machine to critical memory pressure and was killed. The runner is
# waiting on nobody.
#
# A maintainer debugging the GATE ITSELF still needs a local run, and that is
# legitimate — the invocation lives in the workflow, `--copy-vcs true` and all.
# What is not legitimate is a local campaign as the ROUTINE path, and that is
# what this line used to hand people.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# WHAT MAY BE ADDED HERE, AND WHAT MAY NOT
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# An entry is a claim that no test can observe this mutation, with the reason
# stated. There are exactly three admissible reasons, and every line below
# carries one:
#
#   EQUIVALENT   The mutated program computes the same function as the original.
#                No test can ever kill it, because there is nothing to observe.
#                A claim of equivalence must come with its PROOF, not with an
#                assurance.
#   UNREACHABLE  The mutated code has no caller, so no test reaches it. This is
#                dead code wearing a survivor's clothes, and the correct fix is
#                deletion. An entry of this kind is a debt, not a resting place.
#   COSMETIC     The mutation changes only a diagnostic that no contract depends
#                on. Narrow, and easy to abuse — prefer asserting the message.
#
# **A mutation that a test COULD observe is not admissible here.** "Nobody has
# written that test yet" is the one reason this file must never record, because
# recording it converts a missing guard into a documented feature.
#
# **Nor is a known weakness.** If a survivor ever turns out to describe an
# exploitable defect rather than a coverage gap, it does not belong in a
# baseline at all: it belongs fixed, or embargoed. Writing it here would publish
# it and bless it in the same commit.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# ON PUBLISHING THIS FILE AT ALL
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# This is a list of places the tests do not look, checked into a public
# repository for a security tool. That deserves an argument rather than a
# shrug, and the argument is this:
#
#   * It is precomputed, not secret. Anyone can `cargo install cargo-mutants`
#     and derive the same list in under an hour. Withholding it buys time
#     against nobody who is actually looking.
#   * A surviving mutant is a statement about the TESTS, not about the shipped
#     binary. "No test notices if this `<` becomes `<=`" tells an attacker
#     nothing about the program they can run, which contains the unmutated
#     comparison.
#   * The reasons are the part worth reviewing, and a reason can be wrong. A
#     wrong reason is the real risk in this file, and it is a risk that hiding
#     the file makes worse rather than better: an unreviewable justification is
#     how a hole becomes permanent.
#   * Counts alone would not do. A gate that knows only that the number moved
#     cannot tell a closed gap from a new hole, and it names nothing for a
#     person to go and read. That is a gate nobody can act on.
#
# The honest cost: a reader learns which comparisons are unguarded before the
# maintainers necessarily do. That is accepted, and it is why the admission
# rules above are narrow.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# MUTANTS THAT TIMED OUT, AND ARE THEREFORE IN NEITHER COLUMN
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# A mutant that makes a loop run forever is classified by the clock, not by the
# tests. It is not a survivor and it is not caught, so it appears nowhere below
# — and if it ever stops timing out it arrives as a brand new survivor and reds
# a gate that nobody changed. Naming them here is the only way that red is
# recognisable rather than alarming.
#
# The run that produced this file timed out on four, all of them in the two
# loops that count:
#
#   src/audit/mod.rs:  replace -= with /= in AuditLog::write_locked
#   src/mask/mod.rs:   replace += with -= in Masker::scan
#   src/mask/mod.rs:   replace += with *= in Masker::scan   (two lines)
#
# The first is `argv_len -= 1` in the loop that shrinks an oversized row; the
# rest are the scan cursor. Under `/=`, `*=` or a decrement the counter never
# reaches its bound and the loop does not end. These are real infinite loops
# rather than a slow machine, so they time out anywhere, and no test can turn
# one into a normal failure.
#
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# EQUIVALENT. The SHA-256 `Ch` and `Maj` functions, whose operands are chosen so
# that XOR and OR agree on every input.
#
#   Ch  = (e & f) ^ ((!e) & g)
#
# A bit set in `e & f` needs e = 1; a bit set in `(!e) & g` needs e = 0. The two
# operands are DISJOINT, and XOR and OR are the same function on disjoint bits.
#
#   Maj = (a & b) ^ (a & c) ^ (b & c)
#
# Not disjoint, but still equal: both spellings compute the majority of three
# bits. Enumerate all eight assignments and the two columns match — which is why
# the `^` at two separate columns on that one line both survive.
#
# The suite pins SHA-256 against NIST vectors, including the one-million-byte
# one, so anything that changed the digest would die instantly. These do not
# change the digest. There is no test to write.
3	src/audit/sha256.rs: replace ^ with | in compress
# EQUIVALENT. Base64 packs three bytes into one integer:
#
#   let n = (buf[0] << 16) | (buf[1] << 8) | buf[2];
#
# Each operand occupies its own eight bits — 16..23, 8..15, 0..7 — so no bit is
# ever set by more than one of them. On disjoint operands `|`, `^` and `+` are
# all the same function, and both `|` on that line survive for the same reason.
#
# Base64 output is asserted against fixed strings elsewhere in the suite, so a
# mutation that actually changed a byte would be caught. This one cannot.
2	src/mask/encodings.rs: replace | with ^ in base64
